title: Design: LRU Cache
oneLiner: A fixed-size cache that throws out the least recently used entry when it's full -- with get and put both in O(1).
keyTakeaway: Two structures, each covering the other's weakness: a hash map finds a key's node in O(1), and a doubly linked list keeps entries in recency order so moving a node to the front or cutting the oldest one off the back is O(1) pointer surgery. The map stores pointers INTO the list.
explanation:
A cache with room for capacity entries supports get(key), which returns the value or -1 if the key isn't there, and put(key, value), which inserts or updates. When a put would overflow, the entry that was used least recently gets evicted. "Used" means both get and put: reading a key makes it the most recent one. The interview requirement is that both operations run in O(1).

A hash map alone gives O(1) lookup but has no idea which key is oldest; finding it means scanning every entry. A list ordered by recency knows the oldest (it's at the end) but finding a key inside it is O(n). Combine them: keep the entries in a doubly linked list, most recent at the front, and keep a map from key to that key's list node. get looks up the node in the map, unlinks it and re-inserts it at the front. put either updates an existing node (and moves it to the front) or creates a new one at the front; if that pushes the size past capacity, the node just before the tail is the least recently used, so unlink it and delete its key from the map.

The list must be DOUBLY linked: to unlink a node in O(1) you need its predecessor, and a singly linked list would make you walk to find it. Two sentinel nodes, a dummy head and a dummy tail that are never removed, mean every real node always has a neighbor on both sides, so remove and add-to-front are four pointer assignments each with no null checks. Each node stores its key as well as its value, because when you evict the tail node you need its key to delete it from the map.

Most languages ship a shortcut: Python's collections.OrderedDict (move_to_end and popitem(last=False)) and Java's LinkedHashMap with access order are exactly this structure. Mention them in an interview, but expect to be asked to build it by hand, which is what this lesson does. Follow-ups you may hear: make it thread-safe (one lock around both structures, since they must change together), or evict by least FREQUENTLY used instead (LFU, which adds a map from use count to a list of keys).

The harness creates your cache with the given capacity, runs each operation in order with its arguments ([key, value] for put, [key] for get) and returns the list of values your get calls returned. The visualization shows the list from most recent (head) to least recent, with the get results collected underneath.

recognitionSignals: "Design a class" where several operations must ALL be O(1), and one of them needs an ordering (oldest, most recent) that a hash map can't give you.
Bounded memory with an eviction rule based on recency: caches, "recently viewed" lists, browser history with a cap.
gotchas: get must also move the key to the front -- forgetting that turns LRU into "least recently inserted" and fails as soon as an old key is read.
put on an EXISTING key updates its value and refreshes it, but must not count as a new entry or trigger an eviction.
Store the key inside each node: when you evict the tail node you have to delete its key from the map, and the node is all you have.
confusableWith: Hash Maps: Two Sum (Fundamentals) uses a map on its own; here the map is only half the design, and its values are list nodes rather than plain data.

Top-K with a Heap (this track): a min-heap keyed by last-used time also finds the oldest entry, but every access costs O(log n) and updating a key's time inside a heap is awkward. The linked list gets the same ordering for O(1).

complexity.note: Each get or put is one hash-map lookup plus a constant number of pointer changes in the doubly linked list. Space is one map entry and one list node per cached key, so O(capacity).

referenceSolutions.python:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, value):
        self.key = key
        self.value = value
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None


class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.map = {}
        self.head = Node(0, 0)  # sentinel: head.next is the most recent
        self.tail = Node(0, 0)  # sentinel: tail.prev is the least recent
        self.head.next = self.tail
        self.tail.prev = self.head

    def _remove(self, node):
        node.prev.next = node.next
        node.next.prev = node.prev

    def _add_front(self, node):
        node.prev = self.head
        node.next = self.head.next
        self.head.next.prev = node
        self.head.next = node

    def get(self, key):
        node = self.map.get(key)
        if node is None:
            return -1
        self._remove(node)
        self._add_front(node)
        return node.value

    def put(self, key, value):
        node = self.map.get(key)
        if node is not None:
            node.value = value
            self._remove(node)
            self._add_front(node)
            return
        if len(self.map) == self.capacity:
            lru = self.tail.prev
            self._remove(lru)
            del self.map[lru.key]  # the node carries its key so we can do this
        node = Node(key, value)
        self.map[key] = node
        self._add_front(node)
